name: Pongal
cuisine: South Indian (Tamil Nadu; also a Udupi / Matunga breakfast staple in Mumbai)

ingredients.name: Raw rice (sona masoori or ponni, short/medium grain)
Split yellow moong dal (dhuli moong dal / pasi paruppu)
Ghee
ingredients.householdMeasure: 1 tbsp (1 tsp for cooking + 2 tsp for tempering)

ingredients.name: Black peppercorns (kali mirch / milagu)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ tsp, half of it lightly crushed

equipment: Small pan or kadai, for roasting the dal and for the tempering
Mortar and pestle, to crack the pepper
Strainer or bowl for washing rice and dal
Ladle or potato masher (a flat-bottomed steel tumbler or the back of the ladle also works)
Knife, chopping board, measuring cups and spoons (a normal teacup and teaspoons are fine stand-ins)

steps.title: Measure the dal
steps.text: Put 25 g (about 2 heaped tbsp) split yellow moong dal in a small dry pan.
steps.visualCue: A small heap of pale-yellow split lentils.
steps.cameraCheck: The 2 tbsp moong dal in the pan
steps.videoShot: Yellow dal pouring from a spoon into a pan.

steps.title: Dry-roast the dal
steps.text: Roast on low heat, stirring all the time, with no oil.
steps.tip: Roasting is what gives pongal its toasty aroma. If any grains turn brown, the heat is too high; the dal will taste bitter.
steps.visualCue: The dal turns one shade deeper (light golden, not brown) and smells nutty.
steps.cameraCheck: The roasted dal in the pan
steps.videoShot: A spatula moving dal around a dry pan.

steps.title: Add the rice
steps.text: Tip the roasted dal into a bowl and add 50 g (about ¼ cup) raw rice.
steps.visualCue: White rice and golden dal together in the bowl.
steps.cameraCheck: The rice and dal in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Rice pouring onto the roasted dal.

steps.title: Wash rice and dal
steps.text: Cover with water, rub gently with your fingers and drain. Repeat 2 more times.
steps.visualCue: The last rinse water is only slightly cloudy.
steps.cameraCheck: The bowl with the last rinse water
steps.videoShot: Fingers swirling rice and dal in cloudy water.

steps.title: Load the cooker
steps.text: Put the washed rice and dal into the pressure cooker. Add 300 ml water (about 1¼ cups), 1 tsp of the ghee and the 2 g salt. Stir once.
steps.tip: The ghee stops the dal from frothing up and blocking the whistle.
steps.visualCue: The water stands about 3 cm above the grains.
steps.cameraCheck: The open cooker with water, grains and the ghee on top
steps.videoShot: Water pouring in, then a spoon of ghee dropped on top.

steps.title: Pressure-cook
steps.text: Close the lid and cook on medium heat for 4–5 whistles, then switch off.
steps.tip: Pongal needs the rice to be softer than for plain rice, so give 1–2 more whistles than you would for plain rice.
steps.cameraCheck: The closed cooker on the stove
steps.videoShot: Steam puffing out with the first whistle.

steps.title: Let the pressure drop
steps.text: Leave the cooker closed until the pressure falls on its own.
steps.visualCue: The weight lifts easily with no hiss of steam.
steps.cameraCheck: The cooker with the lid off
steps.videoShot: The lid lifting off to show steaming pongal.

steps.title: Chop the ginger
steps.text: Peel a 1 cm piece of ginger (5 g) and chop it finely.
steps.cameraCheck: The chopped ginger on the board
steps.videoShot: A knife mincing a small piece of ginger.

steps.title: Crack the pepper
steps.text: Put ½ tsp black peppercorns in the mortar and give them 3–4 light taps so half are cracked and half stay whole.
steps.tip: Whole peppercorns give soft bursts of heat; cracked ones spread the flavour. Fully powdered pepper makes it harsh.
steps.visualCue: A mix of whole peppercorns and coarse pieces, not powder.

steps.title: Set out the tempering
steps.text: Keep ½ tsp cumin seeds, the pepper, the ginger, 6 cashews, 6–8 curry leaves and a small pinch of hing next to the stove.
steps.visualCue: Small heaps of each, all within reach.
steps.cameraCheck: The tempering ingredients on a plate
steps.videoShot: Overhead shot of the small heaps on a steel plate.

steps.title: Mash the pongal
steps.text: Open the cooker. Mash the rice and dal with a ladle or masher, then stir in 50 ml hot water.
steps.tip: Pongal thickens a lot as it cools. It should look slightly looser than you want to eat it.
steps.visualCue: Soft, creamy and loose enough to slowly drop off the ladle, with a few grains still visible.
steps.cameraCheck: A ladle of pongal lifted from the cooker
steps.videoShot: The masher pressing the rice and dal.

steps.title: Heat the ghee and fry the cashews
steps.text: Heat the remaining 2 tsp ghee in the small pan on medium-low and add the 6 cashews.

steps.title: Add cumin and pepper
steps.text: Add the cumin seeds and the pepper to the same ghee.
steps.visualCue: The cumin sizzles and darkens one shade; the pepper smell rises.
steps.cameraCheck: The cumin and pepper in the ghee
steps.videoShot: Cumin seeds sizzling around golden cashews.

steps.title: Add ginger, curry leaves and hing
steps.text: Add the chopped ginger and curry leaves, stir for a few seconds, then add the pinch of hing.
steps.tip: Stand back a little; wet curry leaves splatter. Add hing last so it does not burn.
steps.visualCue: The curry leaves crackle and turn crisp; the ginger smells sharp.
steps.cameraCheck: The full tempering in the pan
steps.videoShot: Curry leaves spluttering in the pan.

steps.title: Pour and mix
steps.text: Pour the whole tempering, with all the ghee, over the pongal and stir well.
steps.visualCue: Glossy pongal flecked with pepper, cumin, cashews and curry leaves.
steps.cameraCheck: The mixed pongal in the cooker
steps.videoShot: The sizzling tempering poured over the pongal.

steps.title: Check the consistency and salt
steps.text: Taste. If it has thickened, stir in up to 30 ml more hot water. Add a pinch of salt if needed.
steps.visualCue: Soft and spoonable; it settles flat in the bowl instead of standing in a mound.
steps.videoShot: A spoon dropping a soft spoonful back into the pot.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Spoon into a bowl and serve hot.
steps.visualCue: A pale, glossy bowl with golden cashews on top and a ghee sheen.
steps.videoShot: Pongal spooned into a bowl next to coconut chutney and sambar.

reasons: a boiled, not fried, one-pot dish with no onion, garlic or added sugar; moong dal adds easily digested protein, fibre, folate and magnesium, and the bowl is about 435 kcal with about 12 g protein. Against it: white rice makes it starch-heavy with a high glycaemic response, the tbsp of ghee brings about 40% of the day's saturated fat, and salt is about 2 g. Restaurant versions are often much richer in ghee (2+ tbsp a bowl), are saltier, and come with sambar and coconut chutney that add another 150–200 kcal.

researchRating.basis: one of the best-loved South Indian breakfasts, eaten daily across Tamil Nadu and in temples, and the centrepiece of the Pongal harvest festival; the top recipes are very well reviewed (Swasthi's Recipes 4.99/5 from 293 votes) and Mumbai food guides (LBB, Homegrown, HungryForever) single it out at Matunga and Chembur classics such as Cafe Madras, Ram Ashraya and Mani's Lunch Home, and in Rameshwaram Cafe's Mumbai launch coverage. Small deduction because many people find it heavy or bland if under-seasoned, and it is less common on Mumbai delivery menus.

storage: Best fresh; it sets firm as it cools. Fridge: up to 2 days in an airtight box, within 2 hours of cooking. Freezer: possible for up to 1 month, though the texture turns slightly grainy. To reheat, add 2–3 tbsp hot water or milk, cover and microwave for 1–2 min, stirring halfway, or warm in a covered pan on low heat for 3–4 min, stirring.
leftoverRemix: Crispy Pongal Bonda / tikki. Mix 1 cup cold leftover pongal (it will be firm) with 2 tbsp rice flour and 1 tbsp chopped coriander, shape into 4 small flat patties, and shallow-fry them on a tawa with 1 tsp oil per side until crisp and golden (or air-fry at 190 °C for about 12 min). Serve with the leftover chutney: soft breakfast turned into a crunchy evening snack.
burnOff: about 6.2 km of running (435 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 8.7 km of brisk walking (about 1 h 45 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.). With the usual sambar and chutney (about +150–200 kcal), add about 2–3 km of running.

navratri.reason: rice and moong dal (a grain and a pulse) are avoided on the common North and West Indian Navratri vrat rule set; a samak-rice khichdi is the usual vrat swap, but that is a different dish

ekadashi.reason: rice and all dals, including moong, are the main foods given up on Ekadashi

jain.reason: skip the fresh ginger (root vegetable); everything else (rice, moong dal, ghee, pepper, cumin, cashew, curry leaves, hing) fits common Jain practice

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so there is no halal concern; soft, mild and filling, with moong dal protein and slow-release starch, which suits sehri; salt is moderate, about 2 g in the bowl

jain.reason: skip the fresh ginger (a root); add ⅛ tsp extra crushed pepper instead (dry ginger powder only if your family accepts sonth)

vegan.reason: use 1 tbsp cold-pressed groundnut oil (or vegan ghee) instead of ghee

pescatarian.reason: vegetarian, no meat, fish or egg, so it fits a pescatarian diet

sattvik.reason: no onion or garlic; the savoury depth comes from hing, pepper, cumin and ghee

glutenFree.reason: rice and moong dal are gluten-free, but most hing (asafoetida) sold in India is compounded with wheat flour; use a hing labelled gluten-free (rice-flour based) or leave it out

dairyFree.reason: ghee is the only dairy; replace it with groundnut or coconut oil

description: A vegetarian, sattvik (no onion, no garlic) Tamil rice-and-moong-dal breakfast with ghee and pepper; Jain, vegan, gluten-free and dairy-free versions below.
